questions.question: The law of demand states that, other things equal:
options: As price rises, quantity demanded rises
As price rises, quantity demanded falls
As income rises, quantity demanded falls
As supply rises, quantity demanded rises
questions.rationale: The law of demand is the inverse relationship between a good's own price and the quantity demanded, driven by the income effect and the substitution effect.

questions.question: A rise in the price of tea leading to increased coffee purchases shows tea and coffee are:
questions.rationale: Substitutes like tea and coffee replace each other: when one becomes costlier, demand for the other rises.

questions.question: Petrol and cars are complements. If car prices fall sharply, the demand for petrol will:
options: Remain fixed since petrol price is unchanged
Move along the same curve upward
questions.rationale: Cheaper complements boost demand for the paired good: more cars purchased means the whole demand curve for petrol shifts rightward.

questions.question: An increase in quantity demanded (as opposed to demand) is caused by:
options: A fall in the good's own price
A rise in the price of a substitute
questions.rationale: Only a change in the good's own price moves quantity along the curve; all other factors shift the entire demand curve.

questions.question: If the market price is below equilibrium, the result is:
options: A surplus that pushes price down
A shortage that pushes price up
questions.rationale: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied — a shortage — and competition among buyers pushes the price back up.

questions.question: Using the lesson's schedule, at a price of ₹30/kg the mango market shows:
questions.rationale: At ₹30, quantity supplied (20 kg) exceeds quantity demanded (10 kg), creating a surplus of 10 kg that pressures the price downward.

questions.question: Which of the following is a determinant that shifts the supply curve rightward?
options: A growing fashion for the good
questions.rationale: Cheaper inputs, subsidies, and improved technology lower production costs and shift supply rightward; rising incomes shift demand, not supply.

questions.question: If demand and supply both increase simultaneously, the certain outcome is that:
questions.rationale: Both shifts push quantity up, so quantity surely rises; the price effect is ambiguous and depends on which shift is larger.

questions.question: Giffen goods violate the law of demand because:
options: Their income effect outweighs the substitution effect after a price rise
They are luxury status symbols bought for prestige
questions.rationale: For inferior staples like bread in poor households, a price rise so reduces real purchasing power that consumers buy *more* of the staple — the income effect dominates the substitution effect.

questions.question: Veblen goods such as designer diamonds can sell more at higher prices because:
options: They are necessities with no substitutes
Their price itself signals status, raising their appeal
The law of supply applies to them
They are always rationed by government
questions.rationale: Ostentatious (conspicuous-consumption) goods are demanded partly for prestige, so a higher price makes them more attractive — an exception to the law of demand.
